# Fake websites are everywhere


####


Be wary of social media ads offering too-good-to-be-true deals, plus what to do if you’ve been scammed


4 min read


#### KEY POINTS


- More than 40% of people who have lost money to a social media scam said it started when they ordered something they saw in an ad, according to the FTC.
- Ads created for fraudulent purposes may lead to fake websites that often look very similar to the websites that they’re replicating.
- To spot a fake website, look for slightly off URLs, limited contact information and suspiciously high reviews.


We’ve all been there: You’re scrolling through social media and suddenly you see an ad for an item you love and for, wow, what a great price.


It’s tempting to click on that link, right?


Think before you do: More than 40% of people who have[lost money to a social media scam](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/data-visualizations/data-spotlight/2026/04/reported-losses-scams-social-media-eight-times-higher-2020) said it started when they ordered something they saw in an ad, according to a Federal Trade Commission (FTC) report.


Ads created for fraudulent purposes may lead to fake websites that often look very similar to the websites that they’re replicating, experts caution, but ordering from these websites yields very different results. “You make a purchase, but it never arrives, or you receive a counterfeit product,” said Scott Edwards, director of fraud risk management at BOK Financial®.


Fortunately, even though fake websites look similar to the real ones, they’re not exactly the same, so they are detectable. Here’s what to look out for, according to Edwards.


**How to spot a fake website**


1. **Check the URL:** Scammers love tweaking website addresses, hoping you won't notice. Look for misspelled brand names or swapped characters (like "amaz0n" with a zero), extra words or hyphens, and unusual endings like .shop, .store, .deals or .outlet. A padlock icon doesn't mean a site is legitimate. Fake sites can have one, too. When in doubt, type the retailer's web address yourself instead of clicking a link.
2. **Don’t rely on typos to spot a scam:** Fake websites used to be easy to spot because of poor grammar and spelling, but AI now helps scammers produce clean, convincing copy. A well-written site isn’t necessarily a legitimate one. Instead, judge the site on its URL, its payment options and its contact and return information.
3. **Look for limited contact information and shopping policies:** Scammers may only provide an email address and lack customer service phone numbers or chat support. This makes it harder to resolve issues. If you can't find a return policy, you're better off avoiding the site.
4. **They have suspiciously high reviews:** Checking customer reviews can help you sniff out scammers, but AI can now generate fake reviews in bulk. A site with nothing but glowing five-star reviews should be taken with a grain of salt. Look for vague, repetitive praise or a burst of reviews posted in a short window, and check what customers say on independent sites, not just the retailer's own page.


If you’re unsure about the site, do some independent research. Search for the company name plus “complaint” or “scam” to see what pops up.


**Other red flags to watch out for**


Fake websites aren’t the only fraud risks shoppers face, especially during peak online shopping seasons. Here’s what else to be wary of:


- **Too-good-to-be-true discounts:** A website's "60%-off Rolex watches" advertisement should send you running in the opposite direction. Faux e-stores offer popular items at a fraction of the cost to lure in victims. While it's fun to fantasize about the deal of the century, remember that if it's too good to be true, it probably is.
- **Phishing emails and text messages:** Generative AI is making it a lot harder to spot phishing emails and text messages. Beware of unsolicited emails and texts that ask you to click through to the website to make a purchase. Instead, close the email and go to the website through your browser. A common scam around the holidays is “package-tracking” messages directing you to fake shipping sites that ask you to create an account and then steal your personal and financial information.
- **Abnormal payment methods:** Be cautious of websites or customer service representatives that request payment through wire transfers, ACH, gift cards, payment apps (e.g., Cash App) or cryptocurrency, since they are hard to reverse. Instead, stick to well-known payment platforms that offer buyer protection like PayPal and credit cards.
- **Beware of counterfeit products:** Fake goods pose a financial risk for consumers and a health and safety threat, since many products are made with substandard materials or ingredients. Edwards said the best way to protect yourself against counterfeits is to buy directly from the brand and not on third-party sites. Even reputable third-party sellers like Walmart and Amazon may have counterfeit products.
- **AI shopping assistants:** Don’t assume a recommendation is safe. Scammers are setting up fake stores timed to holidays and big sales, and AI shopping tools can sometimes steer you toward them. Treat an AI suggestion as a starting point. Before you buy, visit the retailer’s official site directly and confirm it’s the real one.


**What to do if you are scammed**


If you find yourself in the unfortunate situation of having been scammed, take these steps:


- **Cancel your credit and debit cards and monitor your accounts:** Fake websites are the “gift” that keeps on giving. Once you’ve made a purchase that never arrives, the scammer might also try to make illegal charges on your card or sell your financial and personal information to other nefarious individuals.
- **Contact your card issuer to dispute the transaction:** They may be able to reverse the charges.
- **File a report:** Contact the[Federal Trade Commission](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov/) and the FBI's[Internet Crime Complaint Center](https://www.ic3.gov/default.aspx) . If you suspect your purchase is counterfeit, report it at[www.iprcenter.gov/referral](http://www.iprcenter.gov/referral) .


E-commerce fraud isn’t going away anytime soon. Be aware so you can enjoy fraud-free shopping—and online gift orders that actually arrive.
